The test `test_non_default_dpi` checks whether the figure's DPI (dots per inch) is correctly set to a non-default value. However, the test failure indicates that this is not the case. Following the execution path, we find that when the `fig` object is created using `plt.subplots()`, it inherits its default DPI from `rcParams['figure.dpi']`. Consequently, any subsequent change to the DPI of the figure, such as in line 332 where `bbox2 = t1.get_window_extent(dpi=dpi * 10)`, has no effect on the actual DPI of the figure.

In particular, when we do `np.testing.assert_allclose(bbox2.get_points(), bbox1.get_points() * 10)`, we are comparing the points in the bounding box of `t1` at its original DPI (which is the default) with those at a non-default DPI. This comparison will always fail because the bounding box points have not actually been scaled up by a factor of 10, due to the incorrect DPI setting.

The root cause of this issue lies in the fact that when creating a new figure using `fig = plt.subplots()`, its DPI is set to the default value from `rcParams['figure.dpi']`. This means that any subsequent attempts to change the DPI of the figure will have no effect, as seen in line 332.

To fix this bug, we need to ensure that the figure's DPI is correctly set when it is created. One possible solution would be to pass the desired DPI value explicitly when creating the new figure, like so: `fig, ax = plt.subplots(dpi=100)` (assuming a DPI of 100).

The methods that need to be fixed are:

```
matplotlib.pyplot.figure
matplotlib.pyplot.subplots
```

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
